title: Techno-optimists will doom us all
subtitle: Trump, Musk, and the apocalypse of too much
author: Caroline Ashcroft
introduction: A prominent Silicon Valley billionaire Marc Andreessen stated in his manifesto "there is no material problem - that cannot be solved with more technology". This ideology that now has the ear of President Trump and can be felt in our answer for everything from warfare to climate change. But, writes Caroline Ashcroft, this technological optimism has ideas deeper than a mere fascination for fancy gadgets, it instead forms a part of a totalising world-view about the force that shapes our political possibilities. Drawing on Herbert Marcuse and Hannah Arendt's work in the aftermath of the nuclear bomb, Caroline argues we need to reassert that all technology is political, and that a blind faith in technology can only lead to ruin.
body:
Radical techno-optimism abounds in the twenty-first century. The tech industry proclaims the myriad benefits of its offerings and rejects external oversight and regulation. Venture capitalist and tech billionaire Marc Andreessen’s ‘The Techno-Optimist Manifesto’ offers one particularly extreme version of these claims. “We believe,” he writes, “that there is no material problem – whether created by nature or by technology – that cannot be solved with more technology.” This sentiment lies at the heart of techno-optimism: more technology; technology to solve the problems of technology. While we might be sceptical about the biases of the Silicon Valley elite, there is also a more pervasive optimism about the possibilities of technology. The UK government’s Net Zero Strategy (along with others like it) relies upon the effectiveness of a range of technologies to reduce or balance emissions, and politicians globally see green technologies as a means to mediate between the ever-growing energy demands of industry and economic growth, and the threat of climate change and environmental degradation. Amongst other things, the promise of technology offers a way of sidestepping certain problems, thereby evading the costs of non-technological solutions: social, political, or economic. Technology is the Deus ex Machina of our time.

Modernity’s unquestioned faith in technological progress would result in catastrophe.

A group of political theorists, working in the context of the Cold War, also believed that techno-optimism characterised the world they lived in, and argued that this was a terrible mistake. Thinkers like Jacques Ellul, Herbert Marcuse, Hannah Arendt or Lewis Mumford believed that modern technology posed unprecedented risks to society, and that modernity’s unquestioned faith in technological progress would result in catastrophe. ‘Technology’, in the sense they use it, describes not only technological artefacts, nor even the total aggregate of those artefacts, but a mode of action in the modern world. This idea was described by the French thinker Jacques Ellul as a technique: a “totality of methods…having absolute efficiency…in every field of human activity.” Technology, in such terms, is not a thing (although its character appears in the technological objects we see in the world), but rather a kind of force which exerts its own particular influence upon the world: material, political and ideological, and thus a force which is not entirely within the control of human agency.

Technology, this means, is no longer something we can pick up or leave, a set of useful, although limited tools, but becomes interwoven with almost every aspect of our life.

After the horrors of World War II, and at the dawn of the nuclear age, fear of total warfare played a key role in these theorists’ scepticism towards technology. The paradigmatic catastrophe was nuclear apocalypse. But they believed that modern technology as a whole, and in all its manifestations, was inherently problematic. In media and communications technologies, the capacity for propaganda and surveillance threatened our freedoms, they argued; technologies of production and factory automation increasingly alienated workers from their work. Modern technology operated according to a logic that was continually accelerating, expanding, and ever more totalising and all-encompassing – so that technology is no longer just something in the world, as the anti-nuclear activist and political thinker Günther Anders wrote, but the world itself becomes technology. Technology, this means, is no longer something we can pick up or leave, a set of useful, although limited tools, but becomes interwoven with almost every aspect of our life, such that our relationship with the world (including our social and political relationships) are now mediated through technology at almost every point.

SUGGESTED VIEWING The new ruling class With Yanis Varoufakis

The degree of catastrophism they express may seem somewhat hyperbolic in hindsight. Humanity has not destroyed itself (yet). We still have civil and political rights, freedoms and significant autonomy over our lives, our thoughts and our actions. Yet although the catastrophe these theorists predicted did not come to pass in its most extreme form, their work represents an extended body of thought on the possible threat of technology for a political society that offers an alternative view to technological optimism.

Modern technology has given humans the historically unprecedented capacity to destroy themselves in a number of ways: through nuclear war or accident; global pollution, environmental degradation and climate change; and perhaps we might add to this in the near future, autonomous AI. How might the theorists of catastrophic technology help us to think about the character of these threats in the twenty-first century, or how they might be managed or mitigated?

Technology has not solved the problem of technology, rather the management of nuclear risk is due to political action.

With the benefit of hindsight, it seems there might be scope for cautious optimism. Even with civilisation-ending technologies in the hands of sometimes reckless superpower antagonists, humanity has held back from nuclear warfare. This is however, far from vindicating the techno-optimists. Technology has not solved the problem of technology, rather the management of nuclear risk is due to political action, both from grassroots and governments, that led to non-proliferation treaties, bans on carrying out nuclear tests in the water or atmosphere, and the construction of political norms that places the use of nuclear weapons beyond the pale. Regulation and political cooperation constrained the threat of these technologies of war.

One might also argue that not all technologies can be considered in the same light as military technologies. Many technologies are beneficial and peaceful. The Green Revolution in agriculture, for instance, or antibiotics, have saved millions and unquestionably improved the quality of life globally. The theorists of catastrophic technology, however, made the claim that there is something about modern technology as such that implies extreme risk, both existential and therefore political. They believed that its inherently totalising and all-encompassing nature made modern technology into a fundamentally dehumanising force – the furthering of technology was prioritised above human needs. This, combined with the extraordinary power of modern technologies, created unprecedented and increasing risk, over greater scales of time and space. And if we look at those two examples of antibiotics and Green Revolution technologies, these beneficial technologies have indeed produced what may conceivably become even greater risks in the longer term: the production of antibiotic-resistant bacteria and the deterioration of soil quality. These possibilities do not mean the theorists of catastrophic technology are necessarily right. But their observations might prompt us to ask whether there are intrinsic qualities of modern technology and its utilisation that tend towards particular risks, perhaps related to the sacrifice of the known for the unknown, or the global extension of technological impact.

Yet their analysis of the effects of such machines parallels many contemporary fears about AI: the possibility of devastating, unpredictable, and uncontrollable outcomes in both cases, or the emergence of increasingly autonomous capacity in machines.

What can these theorists, writing in the Cold War, have to say about the risks of AI? Their concerns did not relate to thinking machines, but to doing machines, automated technologies. Yet their analysis of the effects of such machines parallels many contemporary fears about AI: the possibility of devastating, unpredictable, and uncontrollable outcomes in both cases, or the emergence of increasingly autonomous capacity in machines (whether via AI or the logic of technological development itself). Of particular interest is the way that these thinkers conceived the character of this transformation. Although the theorists of catastrophic technology viewed technology as tending to increasing dominance, this trend is not primarily one in which the machines come to dominate us as ‘slaves’ but rather one in which machines transform the world and its possibilities, therefore transforming how humans organise themselves, the possibilities for interactions, relationships and political community.

And while AI in the shape of ‘killer robots’ might grab headlines, if AI does make a substantive impact on the world, it seems that this is a more likely route, if for no other reason than it is much harder to see this taking place and understand the full extent of its effect. Counter-intuitively, the observations of the theorists of catastrophic technology suggest that it might be wise to be alert to the less obviously catastrophic implications of this technology, the unpredicted or even unintended but potentially transformative implications for how human interactions towards one another are influenced.

Hans Jonas writes that he considered his “main fear” with respect to technology to be “the apocalypse of the ‘too much,’ with exhaustion, pollution, desolation of the planet.”

As things stand, the catastrophe that presses upon us with the greatest urgency today is climate change. The critics of technology were extremely aware of environmental threat, and it is here that their technological pessimism seems to speak with greatest clarity to the contemporary world. The rising tide of environmentalism in the 1960s and 1970s was vindication of their ideas. Hans Jonas writes that he considered his “main fear” with respect to technology to be “the apocalypse of the ‘too much,’ with exhaustion, pollution, desolation of the planet.” Certainly, echoes of these thinkers’ ideas can be heard in climate change activism today, its apocalypticism, globalism, and the claim that only radical change will make a difference. Techno-optimism has its own solution to climate change, of course, more technology. Where the critics of technology found in nuclear power a uniquely concerning threat to civilisation (a fear that has largely endured amongst environmentalists), for the techno-optimists nuclear energy is a “silver bullet”; in his manifesto, Andreessen rails against the “bad ideas that effectively outlawed fission.”

SUGGESTED VIEWING Controlling the Tech Titans With Joscha Bach, Roger Hearing, Shannon Vallor, Kenneth Cukier, Alexander Evans

If techno-catastrophism is simply the mirror image of techno-optimism, as this example suggests, why should we take either of these extreme views seriously? The critics of technology realised, unlike the techno-optimists, that technology is political, that it is embedded in contemporary politics, and that in some cases it is becoming an overriding influence on politics. The techno-optimists believe that technology can operate outside the rules and norms of politics, that it can solve its own problems, and that it doesn’t require political oversight or consideration of the ways in which technology has the power to shape the political (for good, or bad). In this, they’re simply incorrect. Because the critics of technology did understand the integral link between politics and technology in the contemporary world – that technology is political – that alone is a good reason for listening to them. One does not have to be as profoundly pessimist as they were, to believe that conscious, political moderation of technological developments, and an awareness of what we are doing to the world, is necessary.

The value of technology is what it can do to benefit humans; an ideology of technology for its own sake stands in opposition to this. A more humanised technology places the ends of human life at its centre. This means recognising that innovation and development in and of itself does not comprise a ‘good’, that democratic and well-informed regulation is essential, and that the direction of technology should not be determined only by the tech industry and its funders.
